passages.t: Grief heavier than the sand of the sea
passages.happening:
‘Then Job replied’ (verse 1). “If only my grief could be weighed and placed with my calamity on the scales” (verse 2). It would be heavier than the sand of the seas, and that is why his words have been rash. “For the arrows of the Almighty have pierced me; my spirit drinks in their poison; the terrors of God are arrayed against me” (verse 4).

A wild donkey does not bray when it has grass, he says, and an ox does not low over its fodder. His loud complaint is a sign that something is truly wrong. The comfort he has been given is like food without salt, loathsome to him.

Then he asks to die: “If only my request were granted and God would fulfill my hope: that God would be willing to crush me, to unleash His hand and cut me off!” (verses 8-9). One comfort is left to him: “that I have not denied the words of the Holy One” (verse 10). “What strength do I have, that I should still hope? What is my future, that I should be patient?” (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
Eliphaz has finished. Job's reply runs through chapters 6 and 7. Here he defends his outburst in chapter 3, describes his pain and turns on his friends. In chapter 7 he will speak to God directly.

Job's images come from the barnyard and the kitchen. Animals complain only when something is wrong. The white of an egg, or by another reading the juice of a plant, stands for the tasteless comfort his friends have offered. His point is that his complaint is in proportion to his pain, and that sufferers are entitled to say so.

Notice that Job blames God directly: the arrows of the Almighty. Unlike the reader, he knows nothing of the accuser, and he does not try to explain God away.

His wish for death is a cry, addressed to God. And even in it he holds on to one thing, that he has not denied the words of the Holy One. His faith is battered, not abandoned.
passages.later: Others in Scripture prayed the same prayer in their darkest hour, and God answered each with care. Jonah said, “And now, O LORD, please take my life from me, for it is better for me to die than to live” (Jonah 4:3).
passages.hard:
Job asks God to crush him and end his life. What does the Bible do with a prayer like that?

Job's words are a cry of pain, not a plan. Several people in the Bible said the same in great distress, among them Moses (Numbers 11:15), Elijah (1 Kings 19:4) and Jonah (Jonah 4:3). The Bible records these prayers without calling them right judgments, and God answers each of them with care rather than condemnation. Job's words show that faith and despair can be present in the same person at once, and that it is better to bring such thoughts to God than to hide them.

The book does not leave Job in this place. He goes on speaking, and in the end God comes to him. The longing for death is real, and it is not the end of his story.

If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today: a doctor, a pastor, a trusted friend, or a crisis line in your country. If you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Job said his complaint was as heavy as his grief. Ask whether you allow yourself, or others, to say how heavy things really are. And if your own longing has turned toward death, ask who you can reach today.

passages.t: Friends like streams that run dry
passages.happening:
“A despairing man should have the kindness of his friend, even if he forsakes the fear of the Almighty” (verse 14). But his friends have been as faithless as desert streams, dark with melting snow in winter, gone in the heat. Caravans turn aside to find them and perish in the wasteland. “The caravans of Tema look for water; the travelers of Sheba hope to find it” (verse 19). They hoped, and they were disappointed. “For now you are of no help; you see terror, and you are afraid” (verse 21).

He never asked them for money or rescue, he says. He asked for loyalty. “Teach me, and I will be silent. Help me understand how I have erred” (verse 24). “But now, please look at me. Would I lie to your face?” (verse 28). “Reconsider; do not be unjust. Reconsider, for my righteousness is at stake” (verse 29).
passages.hearers:
The wadis Job describes are streambeds that flood after rain or snowmelt and then dry out completely in summer. Tema was an oasis town in northwest Arabia, and Sheba a kingdom in the south known for its incense trade. Caravans crossed the desert along routes marked by wells and seasonal streams, and a caravan that counted on water and found none could die. It is one of the finest images in the book: friends who look dependable and fail when they are most needed.

Friendship in that world carried strong duties of loyalty, the word chesed, steadfast kindness, often used of God's own faithfulness. The Hebrew of verse 14 is difficult. Some read it as the BSB does. Others read it to mean that the one who withholds kindness from a friend is the one who forsakes the fear of the Almighty. Either way, Job says the friends owed him chesed, and failed him.

Verse 21 names why: “you see terror, and you are afraid”. His suffering frightened them, and fear made them argue instead of stay.

Job does not claim to be sinless. He says he is in the right in this dispute, tsedeq, and that their accusation is unjust. And he asks them to look at him.
passages.later: A psalm of lament ends with the same loneliness: “You have removed my beloved and my friend; darkness is my closest companion” (Psalm 88:18).
passages.asks: Job's friends were afraid of what they saw in him. Ask whether fear has ever made you keep your distance from someone in pain. And ask what it would mean to look at them, as Job asked, before you speak.
